Background Protein supplements are important to maintain optimum health and physical performance, particularly in athletes and active individuals to repair and rebuild their skeletal muscles and connective tissues. Soy protein (SP) has gained popularity in recent years as an alternative to animal proteins. Objectives This systematic review evaluates the evidence from randomised controlled clinical trials of the effects of SP supplementation in active individuals and athletes in terms of muscle adaptations, metabolic and antioxidant status, hormonal response and exercise performance. It also explores the differences in SP supplementation effects in comparison to whey protein. Methods A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase and Web of Science, as well as a manual search in Google Scholar and EBSCO, on 27 June 2023. Randomised controlled trials that evaluated the applications of SPs supplementation on sports and athletic-related outcomes that are linked with exercise performance, adaptations and biomarkers in athletes and physically active adolescents and young adults (14 to 39 years old) were included, otherwise, studies were excluded. The risk of bias was assessed according to Cochrane’s revised risk of bias tool. Results A total of 19 eligible original research articles were included that investigated the effect of SP supplementation on muscle adaptations ( n = 9), metabolic and antioxidant status ( n = 6), hormonal response ( n = 6) and exercise performance ( n = 6). Some studies investigated more than one effect. SP was found to provide identical increases in lean mass compared to whey in some studies. SP consumption promoted the reduction of exercise-induced metabolic/blood circulating biomarkers such as triglycerides, uric acid and lactate. Better antioxidant capacity against oxidative stress has been seen with respect to whey protein in long-term studies. Some studies reported testosterone and cortisol fluctuations related to SP; however, more research is required. All studies on SP and endurance performance suggested the potential beneficial effects of SP supplementation (10–53.3 g) on exercise performance by improving high-intensity and high-speed running performance, enhancing maximal cardiac output, delaying fatigue and improving isometric muscle strength, improving endurance in recreational cyclists, increasing running velocity and decreasing accumulated lactate levels; however, studies determining the efficacy of soy protein on VO 2 max provided conflicted results. Conclusion It is possible to recommend SP to athletes and active individuals in place of conventional protein supplements by assessing their dosage and effectiveness in relation to different types of training. SP may enhance lean mass compared with other protein sources, enhance the antioxidant status, and reduce oxidative stress. SP supplementation had an inconsistent effect on testosterone and cortisol levels. SP supplementation may be beneficial, especially after muscle damage, high-intensity/high-speed or repeated bouts of strenuous exercise. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s40279-023-01899-w. issue-copyright-statement © Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023 Key Points Introduction Intake of dietary protein is a crucial part of modern nutritional methods, especially to optimise post-exercise recovery [ 1 ]. The most common protein sources used in sports supplementation are whey (a by-product of cheese manufacturing), casein from milk, ovalbumin from egg whites, legumes (mainly soy and peas) and cereal proteins (such as rice) [ 2 ]. Proteins can support the human body to build muscle tissue quicker and more efficiently. Consuming protein-rich supplements as a pre- and/or post-workout supplement can significantly increase muscle protein synthesis [ 3 ]. At a molecular level, protein intake, as well as mechanical loading, stimulates increased rates of mixed skeletal muscle protein synthesis via the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) signalling cascade, a master regulator of protein synthesis that translocates toward the cell periphery [ 4 ]. The peripherical localization of mTORC1 is strategic in human skeletal muscle fibres because of close proximity to focal adhesion complexes and in relation with upstream activators (e.g., Akt), downstream targets [i.e., ribosomal protein S6 kinase beta-1, p70S6K and eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E)-binding protein 1, 4E-BP1], and microvasculature, where L-type amino acid may enter into the fibres [ 5 ]. Recent research evidence that the phosphorylation state of mTOR Ser2448 and p70S6K Thr389 may be further enhanced by protein consumption during the first 2 h of post-exercise recovery [ 6 ]. It is well known that low to moderate level of oxidative stress may provide advantages by improving endogenous antioxidant defences [ 7 ]. However, high-intensity or prolonged exercise may increase exercise-induced oxidative stress, defined as the imbalance between reactive oxygen species and antioxidant defence in favour of oxidants that cause an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the body, thus impairing exercise performance by causing oxidative damage to skeletal muscle fibres or by causing muscle fatigue [ 8 ]. According to some research, the potential impact of soy protein on antioxidant system is attributed to its bioactive antioxidants, including isoflavones [ 9 ]. It is thought that isoflavones exert their beneficial effects as an antioxidant directly by quenching free oxygen species, especially with genistein and daidzein isoflavones, or indirectly by increasing antioxidant scavenging enzymes [ 10 ]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 24 randomised controlled trials on soy isoflavones and oxidative stress biomarkers revealed that soy protein significantly decreased malondialdehyde, a well-known biomarker of oxidative stress, and increased antioxidant biomarkers, including total antioxidant capacity, superoxide dismutase activity and total reactive antioxidant potential compared to the control group [ 11 ]. Another systematic review and meta-analysis of 51 RCTs on soy supplementation and inflammatory biomarkers reported a significant decrease in plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) concentrations after soy, although plasma TNF-α and IL-6 concentrations were unchanged [ 12 ]. One point to consider is that these studies included in these meta-analyses were conducted on either various patients or healthy sedentary individuals. Although soy protein is a promising macronutrient that may improve exercise performance by reducing exercise-induced oxidative stress, to our knowledge, there are no systematic reviews evaluating the effect of soy protein on active individuals and athletes. It is important to critically review the studies which have investigated the effect of soy protein supplementations on athletes and active individuals systematically to suggest its overall influence on antioxidant and inflammatory biomarkers. That is because the effect of soy protein may vary depending on training regimen (e.g., exercise type), duration of intervention, individual’s training/exercise experience, and the effect of timing and dose of supplementation. In recent years, the environmental effect of nutritional supplement production has received a great deal of attention, and there has been a lot of interest in producing proteins from plant-sources rather than those from animals [ 13 ]. Other common reasons that people consume vegetarian products include religious traditions, ethical considerations and health benefits, such as providing a better plasma lipid profile and reducing high arterial blood pressure, thus reducing the risk of cardiometabolic disease [ 14 ]. Considering the high use of plant-based protein sources in athletes in recent years [ 14 , 15 ], several studies have investigated the composition and efficacy of the most common plant-based proteins, including soy, wheat, pea, rice and potato protein [ 16 – 20 ]. Plant-based proteins can include all of the essential amino acids (EAAs); however, they are less abundant compared with animal sources, and the presence of anti-nutrients such as oxalate, phytate, tannins, lectins and trypsin inhibitors that inhibit proteolysis limits their digestion and absorption [ 21 ]. Protein digestibility reveals the fraction of ingested amino acids that can be utilised by the body. Typically, animal proteins are highly digestible (> 90%), rendering them available to be absorbed and metabolized [ 22 ]. Compared with general low-digestibility plant proteins (75–80%), soy protein (SP) may provide advantages with its higher digestibility (95%) [ 23 ] and better composition of EAAs. However, although SPs are considered high-quality protein, they are low in leucine (6%) and sulphur-containing amino acids, such as methionine and cysteine compared with animal-based proteins [ 24 ]. Studies comparing the effectiveness of SP with whey protein have shown equivocal results [ 25 – 27 ]. Although previous research found anabolic superiority of whey protein supplementation [ 28 , 29 ], a meta-analysis of nine long-term studies investigating the efficacy of equal amounts of supplemental soy and animal proteins (a majority from dairy) on muscle mass and muscle strength in response to resistance exercise found no significant difference in lean body mass and strength [ 30 ]. However, studies included in the meta-analysis were mostly (six out of nine) conducted on individuals that did not engage in resistance exercise for more than a year. Furthermore, of the nine studies in the meta-analysis, three favoured animal protein, and six studies showed no significant advantage of either protein type. In none of the studies was soy the superior performer. The ergogenic effect of protein supplementation is well known in sports nutrition; however, the effect of SPs on exercise and sports-related outcomes in active and athletic population has not been comprehensively evaluated. This systematic review aims to discuss the effectiveness of SP supplementation critically and comprehensively on muscle adaptations, metabolic and antioxidant status, hormonal response and exercise performance of active individuals and athletes based on randomised controlled trials. In addition, where applicable, the potential differences between SP supplementation and whey protein supplementation as an animal-sourced protein supplement were discussed.

extracted_data.document_summary: This systematic review evaluates the effects of soy protein (SP) supplementation on muscle adaptations, metabolic and antioxidant status, hormonal response, and exercise performance in active individuals and athletes, often comparing it to whey protein or placebo. The review encompasses studies on protein synthesis, amino acid transport, and signaling pathways, highlighting that while some anabolic markers might be less favorable with soy, it can provide similar increases in lean mass to whey protein, especially at optimal protein intakes. SP is shown to reduce exercise-induced metabolic/blood circulating biomarkers (triglycerides, uric acid, lactate) and improve antioxidant capacity, reducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. However, its effects on hormonal responses, such as testosterone and cortisol, are inconsistent or contradictory across studies. SP supplementation also demonstrates potential benefits in improving various exercise performance indicators, including high-intensity running, maximal cardiac output, delaying fatigue, improving isometric strength, running velocity, and muscle recovery after damage. The review concludes that SP can be a viable alternative to conventional protein supplements, but emphasizes the need for further research addressing methodological limitations and consistent dosing.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Soy Protein and Soy Peptide Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The review encompassed a wide range of soy protein (SP) and soy peptide supplementation protocols, from acute doses (e.g., 15-20g SP, 18g SP beverage, 10g essential amino acids from soy) to chronic daily intakes varying from 0.5 g/kg BW/day to 90 g/day (e.g., 33-40 g/day, 1 g/kg BW/day, 53.3 g/day). Doses were often combined with carbohydrates (e.g., 10g soy peptide + 30g sugar, 15g SP + 52.5g CHO) or matched for nitrogen/leucine content for comparison with whey protein. Durations ranged from single acute sessions to long-term interventions of 2 weeks, 4 weeks, 6 weeks, 9 weeks, 4 months, or even "12 weeks. Comparisons were consistently made against whey protein, soy-dairy blends, isoenergetic placebos, or control (exercise-only) groups. While some studies aimed for optimal protein intakes ("  1.6 g/kg BW/day), there was a notable lack of consistent dosing or explicit dose-response comparisons across the reviewed literature, indicating significant variability in intervention designs.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Promoted the reduction of exercise-induced elevations and significantly decreased in both sexes (more pronounced in men) compared to control groups.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Energy storage, component of blood lipids, linked to metabolic status.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Exercise-induced metabolic response following soy protein consumption; general soy protein supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved metabolic status, reduced metabolic stress during exercise, and improved cardiovascular health.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Promoted the reduction of exercise-induced elevations.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Product of purine metabolism, can act as an antioxidant or indicate metabolic stress.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Exercise-induced metabolic response following soy protein consumption.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved metabolic status and potentially reduced metabolic stress during exercise.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Promoted the reduction of exercise-induced metabolic/blood circulating biomarkers; decreased by 12% (p = 0.003) and decreased compared with control group.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: By-product of anaerobic metabolism, an indicator of muscle fatigue during intense exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Exercise-induced, specifically high-intensity and high-speed running performance; moderate resistance training with SP supplementation; moderate endurance training.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Delayed fatigue, improved endurance performance, and enhanced metabolic efficiency in active individuals and athletes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Better antioxidant capacity against oxidative stress has been seen with respect to whey protein in long-term studies, avoiding a decline in antioxidant capabilities after 9 weeks of strength training compared to whey or control. Increased total antioxidant capacity and total reactive antioxidant potential. Acute supplementation did not prevent exercise-induced elevation of total antioxidant capacity, while glutathione decreased equally among groups.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Defense mechanism against reactive oxygen species and oxidative damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Long-term soy protein supplementation in active individuals and athletes; after speed-endurance exercise; trained weightlifters.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reduced oxidative stress, improved overall health and recovery, especially after high-intensity or prolonged exercise; enhanced antioxidant defense and protection against oxidative stress.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Effects are contradictory: some studies reported fluctuations related to SP, while a 41-study meta-analysis reported no significant effect of SP or soy extracts on total or free testosterone. Other findings include lowered serum testosterone after 2 weeks of SP, no alteration after 12 weeks of SP-based blend, but a significant increase after 4 weeks of soy peptides and 4 months of soy peptides. The testosterone/estradiol ratio increased across all groups with SP and whey.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Primary male sex hormone, involved in muscle growth, bone density, and well-being; influences anabolic processes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy protein or soy peptide supplementation (2 weeks to 4 months) in various active individuals and athletes, sometimes with resistance training; general soy protein, soy foods, or isoflavone extracts supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Inconsistent effects mean no clear indication of consistent benefit or detriment for muscle adaptation or overall health, though some contexts showed increases with soy peptides or an improved androgenic balance.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Some studies reported fluctuations related to SP, and findings were contradictory regarding its effect. Whey protein reduced cortisol's increase during recovery, while SP's specific impact was not consistently quantified.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Stress hormone, involved in glucose metabolism, immune function, and catabolism.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy protein supplementation in active individuals and athletes; during recovery after exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Inconsistent effects mean no clear indication of benefit or detriment for recovery, muscle adaptation, or stress response from this review.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: SP was found to provide identical or similar increases in lean mass compared to whey protein in some studies, especially at optimal protein intakes ("> 1.6 g/kg BW/day). Some studies on untrained individuals reported no difference or minimal positive effects compared to placebo, while others indicated milk/whey might be preferable for faster rates.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Component of muscle adaptation and overall body composition related to physical performance.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy protein supplementation, often in response to resistance exercise, in active individuals, athletes, and untrained participants.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved muscle adaptations and body composition for athletes and active individuals, with efficacy comparable to whey at sufficient intake levels.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly decreased malondialdehyde and lipid peroxidation. Lower serum lipid peroxides from 5 min to 24 h post-workout and decreased after moderate weight exercise training compared with whey. Chronic SP (40 g/day) lowered lipid peroxidation, with antioxidant effects superior to whey.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A lipid peroxidation product, serving as a well-known biomarker of oxidative stress and cellular damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy isoflavones consumption; after moderate weight resistance workout; chronic soy protein supplementation during resistance training.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reduced oxidative stress and cellular damage, indicating improved antioxidant defense and cellular health, potentially reducing the risk of chronic diseases.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reduced serum levels after a month of soy peptides supplementation and lower in SP+sugar group after 4 weeks of strenuous training compared to placebo. However, it stayed elevated after speed endurance training (no significant mitigation by acute SP or whey) and showed no meaningful differences during a 60 min stress test. Improved recovery profile (faster return to baseline) after exercise-induced muscle damage.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An enzyme released into the blood when muscle is damaged, serving as a marker for muscle injury.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy peptides/protein supplementation (acute to 4 weeks/1 month) following various exercises (moderate resistance, speed-endurance, strenuous training, EIMD); 60 min stress test.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced exercise-induced muscle damage and faster recovery in some contexts, but also situations where SP had no significant protective effect on acute muscle damage.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant decrease in plasma concentrations (from previous meta-analyses). However, significantly elevated in both soy-supplemented and untreated groups the day after a field test, and no meaningful differences during a 60 min stress test. Also showed an improved recovery profile (faster return to baseline) after exercise-induced muscle damage.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An acute-phase protein, serving as a general marker of inflammation in the body.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy supplementation (general context, various patients/sedentary individuals); after a field test; during a 60 min stress test; post-exercise muscle damage recovery in boxers.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reduced systemic inflammation in some contexts, but not always mitigating acute inflammatory responses to intense exercise; quicker recovery from exercise-induced inflammation.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Inflammatory Cytokines: TNF-", IL-6, IL-8, IL-10

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Plasma TNF-" and IL-6 concentrations were unchanged after soy supplementation (previous meta-analyses), and no meaningful differences were observed for IL-6 and IL-10 during a 60 min stress test. A small rise in IL-8 was seen in both soy and whey groups during exercise.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Cytokines involved in inflammatory and immune responses (TNF-", IL-6, IL-8 are pro-inflammatory; IL-10 is anti-inflammatory).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy supplementation (general context, various patients/sedentary individuals); during exercise (IL-8); during a 60 min stress test (IL-6, IL-10).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Generally no significant change in these specific inflammatory markers, though IL-8 showed a typical exercise-induced rise.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Synthesis Rate/Synthesis rate/Body Composition/Muscle Adaptation

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Myofibrillar and mitochondrial protein synthesis rates generally showed similar responses between soy and whey protein, or similar benefits with soy + carbohydrates compared to whey. However, some studies reported lower muscle fractional synthetic rates (FSR) with soy protein (e.g., 0.07%/h) compared to milk/whey (e.g., 0.10%/h, p = 0.05), or a 31% greater mixed MPS with whey post-exercise. Conversely, a soy-dairy blend led to a considerably higher (p < 0.05) mixed-muscle FSR (0.087%/h) and a more sustained rise in myofibrillar protein synthesis and S6K1 signaling at 5h post-exercise compared to whey.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicators of muscle protein synthesis and breakdown, determining muscle growth, repair, and renewal of contractile/energy-producing proteins.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Acute and chronic soy protein/soy-dairy blend supplementation (often with resistance/concurrent exercise) compared to milk/whey protein or leucine-enriched SP.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Direct indicators of muscle anabolism, crucial for muscle growth, repair, and adaptation to training, with varying effects depending on protein type and timing.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher/slower initial increase but maintained higher levels
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Postprandial peak plasma leucine concentrations were substantially greater with whey protein compared to soy. However, branched-chain amino acids showed a slower initial increase but maintained higher levels during post-exercise recovery with an SP-based blend compared to whey protein.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Essential amino acids, key signaling molecules for muscle protein synthesis and energy production.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Acute post-concurrent exercise supplementation with whey protein vs soy protein (with/without free leucine); post-exercise recovery comparing SP-based blend with whey protein.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher plasma leucine concentrations are associated with a stronger anabolic signal, while maintained BCAA levels indicate sustained availability of building blocks for muscle repair.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: mTORC1 Ser2448 phosphorylation or signaling showed significant increases in both soy and whey protein groups post-exercise. However, it did not differ between groups after concurrent exercise in some contexts, suggesting similar activation of this key anabolic pathway.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Key regulator of cell growth, proliferation, and protein synthesis; phosphorylation indicates activation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-concurrent exercise acute supplementation with Whey/Soy Protein (+ free leucine); post-exercise recovery comparing soy and whey protein supplementation; following concurrent exercise and ingestion of CHO + whey/soy.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates activation of key anabolic pathways for muscle adaptation and repair, with comparable effects between soy and whey in many contexts.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: p70S6k Thr389 phosphorylation (S6K1) generally showed similar signaling between whey and soy protein. However, one study indicated whey did not enhance S6K1 phosphorylation at 300 min post-exercise, while a soy-dairy blend led to a more sustained rise at 5h post-exercise compared to whey.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Downstream target of mTORC1, involved in ribosomal biogenesis and protein translation; phosphorylation indicates activation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-concurrent exercise acute supplementation with Whey/Soy Protein (+ free leucine); 300 min post-exercise recovery comparing whey protein; post-acute resistance exercise and after ingesting a soy  ffd   dairy protein blend versus whey protein; following concurrent exercise and ingestion of CHO + whey/soy.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates activation of anabolic pathways downstream of mTORC1, with potentially sustained activation with soy-dairy blends.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Anabolic Signaling Proteins: 4E-BP1 Thr37/46 and rpS6 Ser235/236 phosphorylation

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Phosphorylation levels were similar between whey and soy protein groups, suggesting comparable regulation of translation initiation (4E-BP1) and ribosomal function (rpS6).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: 4E-BP1 inhibits translation initiation; rpS6 is a ribosomal component. Phosphorylation indicates activation of protein synthesis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-concurrent exercise acute supplementation with Whey/Soy Protein (+ free leucine); within 360 min post-recovery, following concurrent exercise and ingestion of CHO + whey/soy.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests similar regulation of translation initiation and ribosomal function despite different protein sources, supporting protein synthesis.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Phenylalanine transport and amino acid transporters mRNA

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Phenylalanine transport into muscle was significantly higher with a soy  ffd   dairy protein blend compared to whey protein (p < 0.05). Similarly, mRNA expression of various amino acid transporters (System L amino acid transporter 1 (SLC7A5), CD98/SLC3A2, System A amino acid transporter 2, Proton-assisted amino acid transporter 1, Cationic amino acid transporter 1) was significantly higher (p < 0.05) following a soy  ffd   dairy protein blend, with both soy  ffd   dairy and whey groups experiencing an increase in general amino acid transporter mRNA expression.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Uptake of essential amino acids and peptides into muscle cells, crucial for protein synthesis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise acute supplementation with Soy-Dairy Protein Blend versus Whey Isolate; one hour after acute resistance exercise and ingestion of soy  ffd   dairy protein blend or whey protein.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates enhanced availability and increased capacity for amino acid and peptide uptake into muscle cells, potentially promoting anabolism and muscle growth.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Amino Acid Balance/Amino acid balance measurement

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Considerably longer and more favourable (p < 0.05) during post-exercise recovery following a soy  ffd   dairy protein blend compared with whey protein.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects the net accumulation or release of phenylalanine by a tissue, indicating overall protein turnover and muscle anabolism.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise acute supplementation with Soy-Dairy Protein Blend versus Whey Isolate; post-acute resistance exercise and after ingesting a soy  ffd   dairy protein blend versus whey protein.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A more favorable balance indicates net muscle protein accretion or reduced breakdown, potentially supporting muscle growth and recovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased after 4 months of treatment with soy peptides compared with placebo.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in bone metabolism, liver function, and other processes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy peptides supplementation for 4 months (in the context of Olympic female gymnasts).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potentially indicates changes in bone metabolism or overall health status related to long-term supplementation and physical activity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Tended to be recovered faster with SP supplementation rather than with whey protein or isoenergetic placebo 48 h after speed-endurance exercise. Lower in the soy group (p < 0.004) and tended to be lower in the whey protein group (p < 0.061) compared with the placebo group after speed endurance training.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Markers of oxidative stress and protein damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 48 h after speed-endurance exercise; acute study after speed endurance training comparing whey vs soy protein vs placebo.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a faster recovery from oxidative stress and reduced protein oxidative damage, suggesting protective effects of soy and potentially whey protein.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Downregulated compared with the whey and placebo groups after long-term (4-9 weeks) soy protein supplementation. However, in another context, increased in both whey and training-alone groups, but there were no significant differences with the SP group.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in inflammatory responses and oxidative stress.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Long-term (4-9 weeks) soy protein supplementation in trained weightlifters; after training, comparing whey protein, training-alone, and SP groups.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects reduced inflammation and oxidative stress in some long-term contexts, but no significant difference in others.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased in the supplemented group after 4 months of 1 g/kg BW/day SP supplementation in Olympic female gymnasts.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A hormone involved in various physiological functions, including stress response and metabolism.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Female athletes supplemented with Soy Protein (SP) for 4 months.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a hormonal response to chronic SP supplementation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased in serum levels in the supplemented group, while the non-supplemented group had a decreased level, after 4 months of 1 g/kg BW/day SP supplementation in Olympic female gymnasts.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A thyroid hormone that regulates metabolism, influences physical activity, skeletal muscle development, and muscle regeneration.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Female athletes supplemented with Soy Protein (SP) for 4 months.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates impact on thyroid function and metabolic regulation, potentially influencing physical activity and muscle regeneration, in response to SP supplementation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Plasma insulin response was raised compared with placebo/control groups following acute SP supplementation and soy with carbohydrates after exercise recovery or pre-/during exercise. Soy protein and its peptides can also enhance pancreatic   ffd   cell sensitivity, promoting insulin secretion.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A hormone that regulates glucose metabolism and promotes anabolic processes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Acute SP or SP+CHO supplementation after endurance cycling recovery, after moderate endurance training, or pre-/during exercise; general consumption of soy protein and its peptides.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates an improved glycemic response, enhanced pancreatic   ffd   cell sensitivity, and potential for increased nutrient uptake and anabolic signaling, beneficial for energy metabolism and muscle adaptation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased levels following milk consumption, but no direct effect for soy protein was reported in this context.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Structural component of muscle, linked to strength and power.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following higher dietary protein regimes (~1.6 to 1.8 g/day) with milk consumption.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved muscle composition, potentially enhancing strength or power capabilities, though this specific effect was not attributed to soy protein.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Similar effects on myonuclei content were found between whey and soy-dairy blend supplements.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Support for muscle fiber growth and repair by providing transcriptional machinery.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Comparison between whey and soy-dairy blend supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Myonuclei accretion is essential for long-term muscle hypertrophy and regeneration; similar effects indicate comparable support from both supplements.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Pancreas (functional effect leading to insulin secretion)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Soy protein and its peptides can enhance pancreatic   ffd   cell sensitivity, promoting insulin secretion.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Regulation of insulin secretion, which impacts cellular uptake of amino acids and glucose.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Consumption of soy protein and its peptides.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved insulin response can increase cellular uptake of amino acids and stimulate muscle protein synthesis, supporting muscle adaptation and overall metabolic health.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Conflicted results, with one study showing better V O 2 max after SP supplementation (0.5 g/kg BW/day) in junior judoists, while another found no alteration after soy supplementation (42.2 g SP/day) in trained boxers/road cyclists compared to placebo.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Maximal rate of oxygen consumption during incremental exercise, reflecting aerobic physical fitness.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy protein supplementation (0.5 g/kg BW/day or 42.2 g/day) in junior judoists or trained boxers/road cyclists.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates aerobic capacity and exercise performance, with contradictory findings suggesting context-dependent effects or further research needed.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly decreased low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol (reported in meta-analyses), with effects more pronounced in men than women.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Transports cholesterol to cells; high levels are associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy protein supplementation in post-menopausal women and in both sexes.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved cardiovascular health and reduced risk of chronic diseases.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol (reported in meta-analysis on post-menopausal women).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Transports cholesterol from cells back to the liver; high levels are associated with reduced risk of cardiovascular disease.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy protein supplementation in post-menopausal women.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved cardiovascular health and reduced risk of chronic diseases.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lowered total cholesterol (reported in meta-analyses), with effects more pronounced in men than women. Note that isolated isoflavone extracts, unlike soy protein, did not significantly lower total cholesterol.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Sum of all cholesterol in the blood; a key indicator of cardiovascular health.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy protein supplementation in post-menopausal women and in both sexes.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved cardiovascular health and reduced risk of chronic diseases.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased across all groups (SPs and whey combined with resistance training) in some studies, contributing to an increased testosterone/estradiol ratio. However, a 41-study meta-analysis reported no significant effect of SP, soy foods or isoflavone extracts on estradiol, and it was not significantly altered by SP supplementation in college-aged men.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A primary estrogen, mediates estrogenic effects in humans. Isoflavones in soy may inhibit aromatase enzymes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Non-athletic healthy men supplemented with SPs and whey + resistance training; college-aged men following 12 weeks of resistance exercise; general soy protein, soy foods, or isoflavone extracts supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Influences estrogenic signaling, with inconsistent findings on its direct impact, but can contribute to improved androgenic balance.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: A 41-study meta-analysis reported no significant effect of SP, soy foods or isoflavone extracts on estrone.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A weaker estrogen, primarily produced in fat and muscle tissue.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy protein, soy foods, or isoflavone extracts supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Hormone level, relevant to concerns regarding feminization. No significant effect suggests SP does not impact estrone levels.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: A 41-study meta-analysis reported no significant effect of SP, soy foods or isoflavone extracts on sex hormone binding globulin.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Protein that binds sex hormones (like testosterone and estradiol), regulating their bioavailability.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy protein, soy foods, or isoflavone extracts supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Protein level, relevant to bioavailability of sex hormones and concerns regarding feminization. No significant effect suggests SP does not impact SHBG levels.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No meaningful differences between soy protein supplementation and an exercise-only group during a 60 min stress test.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enzyme indicating cellular damage, particularly muscle damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy protein supplementation (53.3 g protein/day) vs. exercise-only group during a 60 min stress test.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests no significant impact on muscular stress indicators under a 60-min stress test duration.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No meaningful differences between soy protein supplementation and an exercise-only group during a 60 min stress test.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Protein involved in oxygen storage in muscle, released upon muscle damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Soy protein supplementation (53.3 g protein/day) vs. exercise-only group during a 60 min stress test.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests no significant impact on muscular stress indicators under a 60-min stress test duration.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Meaningful increase compared with the control group through strenuous training alone.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Major component of the humoral immune system.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 4 months of soy protein supplementation (1 g/kg BW/day) along with strenuous training in elite female gymnasts.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates enhanced immune function, potentially supporting immune system resilience during strenuous training.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower compared with the control group through strenuous training alone.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Biomarker of metabolic stress.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 4 months of soy protein supplementation (1 g/kg BW/day) along with strenuous training in elite female gymnasts.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced metabolic stress during strenuous training.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased across all groups (SPs and whey combined with resistance training); within-group analysis showed significant increases with soy supplementation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An indicator of androgenic balance, impacting muscle development and other androgen-dependent processes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Non-athletic healthy men supplemented with different combinations of SPs and whey in conjunction with a resistance-training program.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May indicate an improved androgenic balance, potentially beneficial for muscle development and anabolism.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased after training at heavy load.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Subjective feeling of effort or intensity during physical activity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Trained volleyball players (after 4 weeks of 10 g soy peptide + 30 g CHO/day supplementation) after training at heavy load.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates improved exercise performance and reduced fatigue perception during heavy load training.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Enhanced.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: The maximal rate at which an individual can consume oxygen during exercise, indicative of cardiovascular fitness.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Professional junior judoists (after 4-6 weeks of 0.5 g/kg BW/day of SP supplementation).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved cardiovascular fitness and endurance capacity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Enhanced.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: The maximal capacity of the anaerobic energy systems to produce energy during high-intensity, short-duration exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Professional junior judoists (after 4-6 weeks of 0.5 g/kg BW/day of SP supplementation).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved ability to perform high-intensity, short-duration activities.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Improved.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: The ability of a muscle to generate force without changing its length.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Trained boxers (after 4-6 weeks of 42.2 g SP/day supplementation) after EIMD (Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage) exercise; general soy protein supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Enhanced muscle function and recovery following muscle damage.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Muscle Recovery after EIMD exercise/Recovery Kinetics

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Improved muscle recovery and restoration of muscle function following exercise-induced muscle damage. Soy protein can be as effective as whey protein on recovery kinetics if the daily protein intake is adjusted to 1.5 g/kg BW/day.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Restoration of muscle function and reduction of damage following exercise-induced muscle damage; the rate and extent of physiological restoration after exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Trained boxers (after 4-6 weeks of 42.2 g SP/day supplementation) after EIMD exercise; competitive male soccer players after speed endurance training with adjusted protein intake.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reduced post-exercise muscle damage, faster return to baseline function, and improved overall recovery, indicating better adaptation to training stress.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Running Velocity/High-intensity and High-speed Running Performance

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased running velocity compared with the control group, improved running velocity at 2 and 4 mmol lactate thresholds, and improved high-intensity and high-speed running performance (similar to whey supplementation in some contexts and better than placebo).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: The speed at which an individual can run, a key indicator of endurance and athletic performance; ability to maintain high speeds and intensities.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Healthy sports students (after 6-week SP supplementation + moderate endurance training); young adults (after 4 to 6 weeks of SP supplementation with exercise); well-trained/competitive soccer players (with daily protein intake adjusted to 1.5 g/kg BW/day or after speed endurance training).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Enhanced endurance, anaerobic endurance, and speed capabilities, contributing to improved athletic performance and delayed fatigue.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Provided minimal positive effects compared with the placebo group.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: The ability of a muscle or muscle group to exert force.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Young untrained adults (after 6 weeks of 1.2 g/kg BW/day whey or SP supplementation combined with resistance training).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates limited potential for strength gains in this specific population and training protocol with soy protein.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Enhanced/improved.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: The maximum volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute, reflecting cardiovascular efficiency.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Young adults (after 4 to 6 weeks of SP supplementation with exercise); general soy protein supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Enhanced cardiovascular fitness and endurance performance.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Can delay fatigue, thus improve endurance performance compared with both sago starch only and placebo groups.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A state of physical or mental tiredness that limits performance.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Male recreational cyclists (sago + SP supplementation during 60 min of steady-state cycling, followed by a time to exhaustion ride at 90% VO2 max); general soy protein supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved endurance performance.
